segments.title: British global commitments and the naval reversal in 1813
segments.body: Roosevelt criticises Britain's early failure to use its much larger navy effectively against the United States. His assessment is challenged on the grounds that fighting Napoleon and watching several other European navies limited the forces available for America. British 18-pounder frigates subsequently received orders to avoid single-handed engagements with American 24-pounder frigates and to cruise in pairs or small squadrons. More experienced officers and more rigorous practice are also offered as objections to his claim that British gunnery standards remained unchanged. As Napoleon's position deteriorated, Britain could send enough additional ships to impose an effective blockade. Ships of the line then made it increasingly difficult for American frigates to leave harbour.

evidence.note: Roosevelt's criticism of early British performance, the objection about competing European commitments, revised frigate orders, disputed gunnery standards, and reinforcements available as Napoleon's position weakened.

segments.summary: British commitments against Napoleon qualify Roosevelt's criticism of early naval performance, while reinforced squadrons and revised frigate orders explain the reversal in 1813.

segments.title: How the British blockade closed American commerce
segments.body: After May 1813 the blockade was complete from New York southward, with its more severe application to New England delayed until the following year. Roosevelt connects that delay to British hopes that New England's opposition to the war would develop into revolt. Fast privateers and some naval cruisers could still escape, but the risk was too great for ordinary merchant ships. Limited trade remained possible through Spanish Florida and the northern New England coast. Elsewhere, merchant ships lay idle while shipwrights and sailors found work building and crewing privateers. British control of the approaches and estuaries also exposed coastal towns and rivers to attack.

evidence.note: The blockade's geographical expansion, delayed pressure on New England, surviving routes of trade, privateer escapes, idle merchant shipping, and vulnerability of coastal towns and rivers.

segments.summary: The blockade disrupted ordinary merchant trade while leaving narrow opportunities for fast privateers and exposing towns along navigable rivers.

segments.title: Roosevelt's twenty-ship argument for naval preparation before war
segments.body: Roosevelt uses the blockade to argue that a country with a long coastline needs a fighting navy ready before war begins. He contrasts the glory of individual frigate victories with their limited ability to defend commerce and coastal towns. His counterfactual is that twenty capable ships of the line would have made the blockade impossible and averted enormous commercial losses. National resources cannot immediately replace missing ships or inadequate training once fighting has started. The analogy is a prize fighter whose strong constitution cannot compensate for failing to prepare. His use of 'battleships' for ships of the line and 'cruisers' for frigates is interpreted as a way of making the argument familiar to an early-twentieth-century audience.

evidence.note: Roosevelt's preparedness argument, the counterfactual fleet of twenty ships of the line, the limits of national reserve strength, and the connection to contemporary naval spending.
The interpretation that 'battleship' and 'cruiser' make older ship types intelligible to Roosevelt's audience.

segments.summary: A hypothetical fleet of twenty ships of the line connects the losses under blockade to Roosevelt's case for naval investment and training before war.

segments.title: Why did the United States choose war with Britain in 1812?
segments.body: In this interpretation, American leaders expected to seize Canada while France defeated Britain. Britain's European war appeared to create an opportunity for an American attack. The prospect of the French victory on which that calculation rested is treated sceptically.

evidence.note: Canada and the expectation that France would defeat Britain as the proposed explanation for the American decision to fight.

segments.summary: The decision to fight is interpreted as a bid to seize Canada while counting on France to defeat Britain.
segments.question: Why did the United States choose to fight the War of 1812?
segments.answerShort: In this interpretation, American leaders expected to seize Canada while France defeated Britain.

segments.title: Does Roosevelt's War of 1812 history cover the Great Lakes?
segments.body: Roosevelt covers the Great Lakes as well as the oceanic war. He takes a particular interest in the commanders involved in the freshwater operations. The recommendation rests on the book's combination of high-level history and close detail.

evidence.note: Great Lakes coverage, particular interest in the commanders, and the combination of high-level history with close detail.

segments.summary: Roosevelt includes the Great Lakes operations and their commanders, combining high-level history with close detail.
segments.question: Does Theodore Roosevelt's naval history of the War of 1812 cover operations on the Great Lakes?
segments.answerShort: Yes. It covers the Great Lakes, takes particular interest in their commanders, and combines high-level history with close detail.

segments.title: Bad powder and a broken gun carriage doom Gunboat No. 121
segments.body: Ten American gunboats attacked a British brig grounded in Delaware Bay, with a frigate anchored close enough to support her. The Americans' powder was so poor that their officers had already protested that it was unfit for service, and their shots failed to reach the brig. Gunboat No. 121 drifted a mile and a half away from the other boats, giving the British an opportunity to attack her separately. Seven British boats carrying 140 men advanced against her. Her long gun's carriage broke apart at the second discharge, leaving the crew to resist with small arms before the British boarded and captured her. Seven members of her twenty-five-man crew were killed or wounded.

evidence.note: The Delaware Bay attack, previously condemned powder, No. 121's separation from the flotilla, failure of her gun carriage, and capture by British boats.

segments.summary: An isolated American gunboat loses its long gun during a British boat attack, after poor powder has already frustrated the flotilla's gunnery.

segments.title: Asp's survivors return after a British boarding attack
segments.body: Boats from the British brig-sloops Contest and Mohawk attacked the small American gunboat Asp while she was moored in a creek off the Chesapeake. Eleven Americans and eight British were killed or wounded in the fighting before the British captured her and set her on fire. Nine surviving Americans escaped ashore, then returned under Midshipman McClintock after the attackers withdrew. They extinguished the fire, and Roosevelt describes them as restoring the vessel to fighting order. That last claim is questioned because the extent of the fire damage makes her practical ability to fight uncertain.

evidence.note: The capture and burning of Asp, the survivors' return and firefighting, and the explicit doubt about how fully the damaged vessel could resume fighting.

segments.summary: Asp's surviving crew reboarded their burning gunboat after the British withdrew, although the claim that she was ready to fight again is questioned.

segments.title: Surveyor's defence earns the return of her commander's sword
segments.body: Fifty men from the British frigate Narcissus attacked the cutter Surveyor in the York River. Surveyor carried six guns and a crew of fifteen under William Travis. The brief boarding fight left five Americans and nine British killed or wounded. After the capture, the victorious British lieutenant returned Travis's sword with a letter praising both the preparations for defence and the resistance on deck. The tribute recognises how fiercely a much smaller crew contested the boarding.

evidence.note: Surveyor's crew and opposing force, casualties in the boarding, and the letter accompanying the return of Travis's sword.

segments.summary: Surveyor's fifteen-man crew resisted a much larger boarding party fiercely enough for the victorious officer to return William Travis's sword.

segments.title: Alligator repels a night boat attack at the Stone River
segments.body: In January 1814 the American coasting schooner Alligator lay at anchor at the mouth of the Stone River in South Carolina. Her four guns and forty men faced a night attack by boats from a British frigate and brig. The attackers were beaten off with heavy losses, and one British boat was captured. Alligator lost two men killed and two wounded. The opposing British ships are left unnamed in the account.

evidence.note: Alligator's armament and crew, the night boat attack, American casualties, capture of an attacking boat, and the absence of names for the British parent ships.

segments.summary: Alligator's small crew beat off British boats after dark and captured one of the attacking craft.

segments.title: Could a Clemson-class destroyer sink a wooden first rate?
segments.body: The hypothetical matchup assumes a Clemson-class destroyer of the First World War era, armed with four-inch guns. High-explosive ammunition is expected to destroy the wooden first rate very quickly. Armour-piercing shells might pass through the wooden hull and emerge from the other side, making their destructive effect less certain. Modern guns also allow the destroyer to engage beyond the sailing ship's effective range. A further suggestion is that star shell could set L'Orient on fire, making ammunition choice central to the comparison.

evidence.note: Identification of the intended Clemson-class destroyer and the different expected effects of high-explosive and armour-piercing ammunition on L'Orient.
Star shell proposed as another means of setting the wooden ship on fire.

segments.summary: Four-inch ammunition choice governs this counterfactual fight: high-explosive shells should devastate L'Orient, while armour-piercing rounds might pass through its wooden hull.
segments.question: How quickly would a Clemson-class destroyer sink a 120-gun ship of the line such as L'Orient?
segments.answerShort: High-explosive ammunition is expected to destroy L'Orient very quickly; armour-piercing rounds might pass through its wooden hull with less destructive effect.

segments.title: Could USS Gearing defeat HMS Victory without torpedoes?
segments.body: The hypothetical fight excludes torpedoes. With modern guns and high-explosive shells, Gearing could remain beyond Victory's effective range and bombard the sailing ship. Only a few hits are expected to be needed, especially if a shell reaches the powder.

evidence.note: The no-torpedoes condition, modern gun range, and expected effects of high-explosive shells on Victory.

segments.summary: Gearing's modern guns and high-explosive shells are expected to decide the counterfactual fight from beyond Victory's range.
segments.question: Who would win between USS Gearing and HMS Victory without torpedoes, and how long would it take?
segments.answerShort: With high-explosive ammunition, Gearing could stay outside Victory's range and destroy her with a few hits, especially if it struck the powder.

segments.title: Modern Naval Strategy charts the battleship cost spiral
segments.body: Modern Naval Strategy, published in 1940, compares battleships by launch date, displacement, length, armament, speed, and cost. Its table begins with Victory at 2,164 tons and £100,000, then follows the growth of steam battleships through Alexandra, Camperdown, Lord Nelson, Dreadnought, and Nelson. Lord Nelson appears at 16,500 tons and £1.6 million, while Dreadnought is listed at 17,900 tons and £1.8 million. Nelson reaches 33,950 tons and £7.5 million, with nine sixteen-inch guns. The authors use the table to show that displacement roughly doubled after 1906 while cost increased much faster. Heavier guns and larger ships therefore brought a substantial increase in the financial burden of a battle fleet.

evidence.note: The 1940 book's battleship comparison table and its conclusion about rising displacement, gun calibre, and cost between 1906 and 1925.

segments.summary: A comparison of Victory, Alexandra, Camperdown, Lord Nelson, Dreadnought, and Nelson shows battleship costs rising faster than displacement.

segments.title: Why Modern Naval Strategy ties battleships to an enemy battle fleet
segments.body: Modern Naval Strategy argues that battleships are primarily needed to fight other battleships. If every battle fleet disappeared, superiority in other kinds of ship would determine command of the sea. The authors connect this argument to the difficulty of constructing capital ships quickly enough to surprise an opponent during a war. Smaller vessels create a different planning problem because they can be built more rapidly on smaller slips, with construction potentially disguised as merchant work. Navies therefore need to build their smaller forces in peacetime to meet wartime requirements.

evidence.note: The authors' argument about battleships countering battleships, capital-ship construction time, and the different wartime building possibilities for smaller vessels.

segments.summary: The book relates the purpose of a battle fleet to opposing battleships and distinguishes capital-ship construction from the quicker expansion of smaller forces.

segments.title: Barham and Admiral Scheer test the case for smaller battleships
segments.body: The proposal to build two smaller battleships for the price of one large ship encounters several physical limits. Armour needs displacement to support it, machinery needs space and weight, and hull length helps a ship maintain speed in a seaway. Modern Naval Strategy compares Admiral Scheer and Barham to examine the tradeoff. Its figures contrast Scheer's six eleven-inch guns with Barham's eight fifteen-inch guns and compare their armour, speed, and displacement. The authors conclude that one Barham is worth three Scheers. The comparison is challenged at its starting point because Scheer is a heavy cruiser rather than a battleship.

evidence.note: Arguments for and against smaller battleships, physical demands of armour and speed, the Barham-Scheer comparison, its stated conclusion, and the objection to classifying Scheer as a battleship.

segments.summary: Armour, machinery, hull length, and gun power complicate the claim that several smaller ships can replace a large battleship at equal cost.

segments.title: Reading Modern Naval Strategy as evidence of interwar thinking
segments.body: A strategy book can reveal contemporary naval thinking even when its conclusions remain open to strong disagreement. Modern Naval Strategy receives a qualified recommendation on those grounds. Its authors are described as well informed, although they were behind the newest developments when they wrote it. Their arguments help explain ideas circulating in the 1920s and 1930s.

evidence.note: The recommendation to read the book despite disagreement, based on its authors' knowledge and its value for understanding interwar naval ideas.

segments.summary: A qualified recommendation treats the book as evidence of interwar naval thinking despite substantial disagreement with its conclusions.

segments.title: Could Admiral Scheer handle alert coastal battleships?
segments.body: The proposed matchup depends on whether the Scandinavian coastal battleships are already alert and ready to fire. Scheer might be unable to defeat them under those conditions.

evidence.note: The claim that Scheer could handle Scandinavian coastal battleships and the conditional objection about opponents already alert and ready to fire.

segments.summary: The claim that Scheer could defeat Scandinavian coastal battleships is qualified by whether those opponents were alert and ready to open fire.
segments.question: Could Admiral Scheer handle Scandinavian coastal battleships?
segments.answerShort: Possibly not if the coastal battleships were alert and ready to fire immediately.

segments.title: Serbia's alternatives when answering the July Crisis ultimatum
segments.body: Clive Ponting's 13 Days examines the diplomatic choices between the Sarajevo assassination and the outbreak of war. One proposed Serbian response was to accept Austria-Hungary's ultimatum in principle, then negotiate its complex details while other governments applied pressure to Vienna. In the book's account, Belgrade faced humiliation, anger from extreme nationalists, and the risk of revealing connections between parts of the government and the Sarajevo conspiracy. Uncertainty about Russian support also affected how far Serbia was prepared to concede. The cabinet instead sought to appear as accommodating as possible while openly rejecting the participation of Austro-Hungarian officials in the judicial inquiry. Qualifications on most of the other points would have left room to avoid implementing demands even if Vienna accepted the reply.

evidence.note: Introduction to 13 Days and its focus on the diplomatic decisions between the assassination and the outbreak of war.
Acceptance in principle as an alternative, domestic and diplomatic constraints, Russian support, rejection of foreign participation in the inquiry, and qualifications within the other concessions.

segments.summary: Serbia faced a choice between outright rejection, acceptance followed by negotiation, and carefully qualified concessions.

segments.title: Serbia's reply denies responsibility while promising prosecutions
segments.body: Serbia's reply presents its recent policy as peaceful and cooperative, citing earlier settlements with Austria-Hungary. It denies responsibility for private newspaper articles and societies that ordinarily fall outside official control. The government expresses surprise at allegations connecting Serbian subjects to the Sarajevo crime, while offering to try anyone whose complicity can be proved. It also promises a public declaration condemning propaganda aimed at detaching territory from Austria-Hungary. Its acknowledgement concerning officers and officials remains tied to the accusations communicated by Vienna. The declaration closes with a warning that officials and the wider population will face measures against such activity.

evidence.note: Serbia's account of its earlier conduct, denial of responsibility for private activity, conditional offer to prosecute, and proposed declaration against anti-Austrian propaganda.

segments.summary: The Serbian reply combines claims of peaceful conduct with denials of responsibility, conditional prosecutions, and a promised declaration against anti-Austrian propaganda.

segments.title: The legal qualifications in Serbia's promise to suppress hostile publications
segments.body: Serbia undertakes to publish its declaration through an army order issued in the king's name by Crown Prince Alexander. The reply also promises severe penalties for incitement to hatred or contempt of Austria-Hungary. Those penalties require a provision to be introduced when the national assembly next meets. Confiscating hostile publications additionally depends on an amendment to Article 22 of the constitution. The promise therefore incorporates future legislative and constitutional steps into its implementation.

evidence.note: Publication through the army, proposed press-law penalties at the assembly's next regular session, and the constitutional amendment required for confiscating publications.

segments.summary: Promises to punish hostile publications depend on later changes to the press law and constitution, illustrating the qualifications within Serbia's concessions.

segments.title: The Darkest Days and Ponting's account of Serbia
segments.body: The Darkest Days and Clive Ponting's 13 Days are both recommended. Ponting's book is preferred for the particular question about Serbia being researched because its treatment of the Serbian side is considered stronger.

evidence.note: Recommendation of The Darkest Days alongside Ponting's account, with a stated preference for Ponting's Serbian coverage for the question being researched.

segments.summary: Both books receive a recommendation, with Ponting's account preferred here for its coverage of Serbia.
segments.question: Have you read The Darkest Days on the same subject as Clive Ponting's 13 Days?
segments.answerShort: Yes, and it is worth reading. Ponting's account is preferred here for its treatment of the Serbian side.

segments.title: A Midway anthology built from specialists and participants
segments.body: Thomas C. Hone's Midway anthology combines specialist scholarship with accounts by officers who participated in the battle. Its selections include Naval Institute articles, oral history, and contributions from Spruance and Layton. Different contributors handle the subjects they know best, allowing operational decisions to be examined from several positions within the battle. The collection also preserves earlier work by participants who were no longer alive when the volume was assembled. Jimmy Thach's 'Flying into a Beehive' is selected for the reading that follows.

evidence.note: Editorial selection of specialists, Naval Institute articles, and participant accounts, followed by the choice of Jimmy Thach's oral history.

segments.summary: Thomas C. Hone's Midway anthology combines specialist scholarship with participant accounts, including Spruance, Layton, and Jimmy Thach.

segments.title: Why Jimmy Thach chose to escort Yorktown's torpedo bombers
segments.body: Jimmy Thach recalled having too few fighters to protect both Yorktown's dive bombers and torpedo bombers at Midway. The squadron commanders initially tried to assign the scarce escort to each other's aircraft. Thach chose the torpedo force because he expected Japanese fighters to concentrate on an attack that had proved dangerous at the Coral Sea. The slow TBD Devastators lacked self-sealing fuel tanks and needed protection during their approach. He feared that a combined Japanese combat air patrol would heavily outnumber the escort and that the Zero's performance would prevent the Wildcats from using their better guns effectively. The expectation of tactical surprise nevertheless gave the pilots confidence before the attack.

evidence.note: Thach's recollection of escort allocation, the Coral Sea precedent, TBD vulnerability, Japanese fighter strength, and anticipated tactical surprise.

segments.summary: Yorktown's scarce Wildcats accompanied the vulnerable TBD Devastators because Thach expected Japanese fighters to concentrate on the torpedo attack.

segments.title: Fitting six Wildcats around a slow torpedo formation
segments.body: Yorktown's separation from Enterprise and Hornet worried Jimmy Thach because the carriers needed mutual defensive support. A late decision reduced his escort from eight Wildcats to six, disrupting the four-aircraft divisions he had intended to use. He placed four fighters above the torpedo bombers and assigned the remaining pair a lower position astern. The Wildcats flew S-turns to stay with the much slower TBDs while retaining enough speed to manoeuvre if attacked. His last briefing stressed keeping the formation together because an isolated fighter was unlikely to survive the expected opposition.

evidence.note: Thach's recollection of separated carrier groups, the reduction to six escorts, fighter positions around the TBDs, S-turns, and formation discipline.

segments.summary: A late cut to six Wildcats forced a four-plus-two escort arrangement, while S-turns kept the fighters beside the slower TBDs without sacrificing manoeuvring speed.

segments.title: Why the Thach Weave used four fighters in two sections
segments.body: Thach's formation divided four fighters into two sections, each consisting of a leader and one wingman. Before the war, the two-aircraft section was considered too radical to impose across every squadron, although he received permission to use it in his own. Other squadrons began abandoning the third aircraft in each section without necessarily adopting the weaving manoeuvre. James Flatley proposed trying a six-aircraft formation alongside Thach's four-aircraft arrangement. In Thach's recollection, Flatley later reported that the extra pair became lost and endorsed the four-aircraft division and the Thach Weave for fighting superior enemy aircraft.

evidence.note: Thach's recollection of authorisation for two-plane sections, uneven adoption, and Flatley's comparison of four- and six-aircraft formations.

segments.summary: Adopting two-plane sections and adopting the weaving manoeuvre were separate steps; Flatley's reported comparison supported a four-aircraft division.

segments.title: Why the Thach Weave did not transfer neatly to the Bf 110
segments.body: One suggested explanation for the Bf 110 comparison is that the Thach Weave depended on a particular relationship between opposing fighters. An attacker fixated on one aircraft would follow it into the line of fire of its partner. The Bf 110's encounters with Spitfires, Hurricanes, Gladiators, MiGs, and Yaks did not offer the same favourable circumstances. Aircraft performance and pursuit behaviour therefore affected whether the crossing manoeuvre could provide mutual support.

evidence.note: Viewer's report of finding no comparable Bf 110 formation and a proposed explanation based on the fighter types and pursuit behaviour involved.

segments.summary: The proposed explanation turns on whether an attacking fighter can be drawn into another aircraft's fire, and whether the Bf 110's opponents offered that opportunity.
segments.question: Why might Bf 110 units not have developed formation tactics similar to the Thach Weave?
segments.answerShort: The suggested reason is that the Bf 110 faced different opponents and performance relationships, making the same crossing mutual-support tactic less attractive.

segments.title: Would an Arethusa-class cruiser be a better choice at Narvik?
segments.body: In this Narvik counterfactual, an Arethusa-class cruiser is preferred because British destroyers already supply substantial 4.7-inch fire. Atlanta or Dido would add more rapid fire when heavier shells would be more useful. Arethusa's six-inch guns combine that extra hitting power with manoeuvrability in the fjord. Warspite also went farther up the fjord than a postwar chart shows.

evidence.note: Hypothetical Atlanta deployment compared with Arethusa's six-inch armament, existing destroyer firepower, and Warspite's movement in the fjord.

segments.summary: For a counterfactual Narvik deployment, an Arethusa-class light cruiser offers more useful hitting power than Atlanta or Dido because its six-inch guns complement the destroyers' rapid fire.
segments.question: Would taking an Atlanta-class cruiser to the battles of Narvik be useful?
segments.answerShort: An Arethusa-class cruiser is the preferred choice in this counterfactual because its six-inch guns add heavier shells while British destroyers already supply rapid 4.7-inch fire.

segments.title: Comparing Roosevelt's naval ideas with the policies he carried out
segments.body: Roosevelt's own writing can be compared with Henry Hendrix's study of his naval diplomacy to examine the relationship between stated ideas and action. Many naval theorists never receive the authority to build the forces they propose. Decision-makers with that authority do not always leave a clear written account of their theories. Roosevelt supplies both kinds of material, but his ability to promote a public vision requires care when comparing his claims with what he actually did.

evidence.note: Comparison of Roosevelt's published ideas with Hendrix's examination of his actions, including the distinction between public presentation and practice.

segments.summary: Pairing Roosevelt's own writing with a study of his diplomacy allows his stated naval ideas to be compared with decisions made in office.

segments.title: Roosevelt's private warnings in Hendrix's account of the Venezuela crisis
segments.body: In Henry Hendrix's account, Roosevelt regarded Germany's naval expansion and activity overseas as a challenge to the Monroe Doctrine. A letter to Henry Cabot Lodge connects a larger American navy with the ability to resist a German move in the West Indies or South America. During the Venezuela crisis, formal diplomatic contacts and private messages accompanied preparations for a force commanded by Admiral Dewey. A ten-day deadline was subsequently shortened, and Germany accepted arbitration after its ambassador conveyed the seriousness of the warning. In this interpretation, keeping the demands private allowed Wilhelm to retreat without the public humiliation that could have made war more likely.

evidence.note: Henry Hendrix's account of Roosevelt's assessment of Germany, the Monroe Doctrine, Dewey's force, private deadlines, and arbitration.

segments.summary: Hendrix's account connects a private ultimatum and Dewey's fleet with German acceptance of arbitration during the Venezuela crisis.

segments.title: British food imports and the risk of a second war across the Atlantic
segments.body: British planning during the Venezuela crisis considered whether possessions in the western Atlantic could be defended against the United States. The Admiralty doubted that it could send enough ships to secure the western Atlantic and Caribbean while also facing uncertain or hostile relations with a European power. A memorandum quoted by Hendrix added that the United States could interrupt supplies from Canada and halt its own food exports to Britain. Its estimate put two-thirds of Britain's food supply at risk. Hendrix connects these naval and commercial vulnerabilities with the British conclusion that good relations with the United States had to be preserved.

evidence.note: British memorandum quoted in Hendrix's account, covering simultaneous European and American threats, western Atlantic defence, and an estimated two-thirds food-supply exposure.

segments.summary: A British memorandum linked limited fleet availability with dependence on Canadian and American food supplies during a possible Atlantic war.

segments.title: Panama's revolt and the evidence for War Portfolio Number One
segments.body: The proposed Panama Canal would allow U.S. warships to transfer quickly between the Atlantic and Pacific, increasing the usefulness of the available fleet. Colombia's rejection of the canal treaty put that project in doubt. Henry Hendrix distinguishes the Panamanian revolutionaries' decision to revolt from Roosevelt's response once the uprising began, noting the absence of evidence for an explicit advance promise of assistance. His account leaves open whether the movement represented a broad popular uprising or a smaller group of business and intellectual interests. Military records identify actions by two American army officers and a U.S. warship off Panama, alongside War Portfolio Number One. That contingency plan envisaged American military defence of a new Panamanian republic and provides evidence of preparations beyond the administration's public statements.

evidence.note: Canal fleet-transfer advantages, limits of evidence for advance promises to rebels, unresolved questions about the revolt's support, and War Portfolio Number One in Hendrix's account.

segments.summary: Hendrix separates the uncertain origins of Panama's revolt from the documented American contingency plan to defend a new republic.

segments.title: Payments and sovereignty in the Hay-Herran Treaty dispute
segments.body: In Hendrix's account, opposition to the canal treaty combined Colombian sovereignty concerns with demands for higher payments. A confidential American warning reached Colombian senators and intensified the dispute. Proposed amendments would require the French canal company to pay Colombia $10 million from its $40 million sale proceeds and increase the direct American payment from $10 million to $15 million. The United States had already accepted a hundred-year term, a zone ten kilometres wide, and a rise from its initial $7 million offer to $10 million. Secretary of State Hay rejected imposing the additional financial obligation on the French company, and Roosevelt would not reopen those terms. The Colombian Senate's rejection in August ended this stage of the negotiations.

evidence.note: Hendrix's account of sovereignty objections, the leaked American warning, proposed additional payments, earlier concessions, Hay's refusal, and Colombian Senate rejection.

segments.summary: The canal negotiations stalled over Colombian sovereignty and additional payments after the United States had accepted several changes to the original terms.

segments.title: Britain's Naval Future defines limited sea control
segments.body: James Cable defines sea control through the ability to use maritime communications and deny their use to an opponent. He treats that control as a condition for other naval tasks and sustained joint operations, including the projection of power ashore. Even a clearly superior navy cannot expect control to be complete, permanent, or universal. British dominance during the Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars still permitted substantial losses to commerce raiders, while U-boats threatened Britain with defeat in the First World War. The time needed to establish American control in the Pacific and a brief failure of British control around Norway illustrate the consequences of delay or interruption. Available resources, the particular conflict, and the importance of each maritime activity determine how control can be exercised.

evidence.note: Cable's definition of sea control and its limits, illustrated by commerce raiding, U-boats, the Pacific campaign, and Norway.

segments.summary: James Cable treats sea control as the ability to use maritime communications, with practical limits set by time, geography, opponents, and available forces.

segments.title: A battle fleet built for a blockade that never came
segments.body: Cable locates some wartime naval shortages in mistaken expectations about the conflict, as well as technical errors and resource constraints. Before the First World War, both British and German naval leaders had received substantial political support for their programmes. Germany's battle fleet nevertheless lacked a workable answer when Britain imposed a distant blockade instead of the close blockade anticipated by German planning. That left the fleet unable to reach the system it had been built to defeat. Cable also criticises Britain's failure to anticipate submarine warfare against trade and its delayed return to convoy and escort.

evidence.note: Cable's criticism of prewar strategic assumptions, the High Seas Fleet's intended response to close blockade, distant blockade, and Britain's delayed convoy response.

segments.summary: Cable argues that German planning expected a close blockade, while British planning underestimated the submarine threat to trade.

segments.title: Cable's criticism of Britain's prewar allocation of resources
segments.body: James Cable argues that the later arrival of powerful allies obscured weaknesses in Britain's original strategy for the Second World War. The expeditionary army and long-range bombers had failed to achieve their initial purposes of deterring Germany and preventing its conquest of Europe. In his assessment, resources devoted to those commitments left too few suitable ships and aircraft to defend Britain and its sea routes. He considers an earlier maritime strategy intended to secure Britain until circumstances offered a better prospect of defeating Germany. He cannot prove the outcome of that alternative, or that maritime defence and the adopted commitments were necessarily mutually exclusive. His criticism concerns the risks and opportunity costs of Britain's strategic choices.

evidence.note: Cable's argument about deterrence failures and competing resource demands, followed by his explicit limits on proving a maritime-strategy counterfactual.

segments.summary: Cable questions the resources committed to the expeditionary army and bombing, while admitting that the outcome of his proposed maritime alternative cannot be proved.

segments.title: Why preventing invasion matters more than every hostile passage
segments.body: Political objectives determine which uses of the sea are decisive in a particular war. Cable contrasts denying the Channel to an invasion force in 1588, 1688, or 1940 with the German warships' return through it in February 1942. The latter passage humiliated Britain without deciding the war, so the two kinds of failure had very different consequences. He challenges theories that make command of the sea an end in itself instead of asking what it must accomplish. His criticism extends to Corbett's dismissal of trade destruction as the expedient of an inferior navy and to assumptions that moral objections would prevent attacks on merchant ships. The effectiveness of sea denial has to be judged against the conflict's objectives and the consequences for the opponent.

evidence.note: Cable's comparison of invasion prevention with the February 1942 Channel passage and his criticism of command-of-the-sea theory and assumptions about attacks on trade.

segments.summary: Cable distinguishes decisive control, such as stopping an invasion, from a temporary enemy passage that humiliates a navy without deciding the conflict.

segments.title: Did the Black Buck raids materially change the Falklands War?
segments.body: Black Buck's main benefits are assessed as psychological pressure and the diversion of Argentine fighters northward. Hercules transports continued to reach Stanley at night, so the raid did not sever the air bridge. The extent of the runway damage remains uncertain in this assessment: it was either not hit as claimed or repaired rapidly enough for transport flights to continue. A runway extension suitable for fighters is also considered unlikely once the blockade was in place. The distinction is therefore between a useful psychological and diversionary effect and the stronger claim that physical damage to the airfield helped decide the war.

evidence.note: Competing assessments of Black Buck, continued Hercules flights, uncertain runway damage or rapid repair, and the relocation of Argentine fighters.

segments.summary: The assessment credits Black Buck with psychological pressure and diverted Argentine fighters while questioning decisive runway damage or interruption of the air bridge.
segments.question: Were the Black Buck raids worth their cost, and did the hit on Stanley's runway materially help win the Falklands War?
segments.answerShort: Psychological pressure and diverted Argentine fighters were the strongest benefits identified; continued Hercules flights undermine the claim that runway damage severed the air bridge.

segments.title: What should the Royal Navy have changed after the Falklands War?
segments.body: The Leander-class frigates had been successful mass-produced ships in their own period, but their capabilities no longer suited the tasks imposed on them in the Falklands War. Fleet recapitalization brought Type 23s and increased Type 22 numbers. A Type 43 would have been a preferred addition, though the actual fleet received longer Type 42s. Naval cuts had continued under successive governments because Cold War planning prioritized NATO's central front. Michael Clapp recalled being discouraged from practising convoy operations on the grounds that a nuclear war would end before a convoy arrived. That assumption left other kinds of war outside the dominant planning model.

evidence.note: Leander limitations, Type 22 and Type 23 recapitalization, the preferred Type 43 alternative, and Michael Clapp's recollection of opposition to convoy practice.

segments.summary: Ageing Leanders and neglected convoy practice illustrate the weaknesses of preparing the Royal Navy primarily for a short central-front war.
segments.question: After the Falklands War, which Royal Navy decisions should have been retained or expanded, and what should have been replaced?
segments.answerShort: Replace outdated ships with modern Type 22 and Type 23 frigates, consider the preferred Type 43 alternative, and preserve the ability to fight wars beyond the central NATO scenario.

segments.title: Broad-beamed Type 22s, larger Invincibles, and a Type 82 fleet escort
segments.body: Clarke's father, who worked on Type 22 and Type 23 frigates, favoured larger Invincibles and continued Bristol construction. He regarded the Invincible class as fairly good and wanted a stretched version with more aviation space and deck-edge lifts. The proposed length increase is recalled as roughly twenty to twenty-five metres. He also preferred Bristol-derived escorts with combined Sea Dart and Sea Wolf defences instead of the smaller Type 42s. A pair of these escorts with each Invincible, whose own Sea Dart launcher added another layer, could form an effective carrier force. Frigates would then have greater freedom to concentrate on anti-submarine warfare.

evidence.note: Type 22 and Type 23 design work and a father's preferences for stretched Invincibles and continued Bristol construction.
Recollection of a Bristol modification combining Sea Dart and Sea Wolf before the decision to build Type 42s.
Paired escorts and each Invincible's own Sea Dart launcher would strengthen the carrier force and free frigates for anti-submarine duties.

segments.summary: Longer Invincibles and Bristol-derived escorts with Sea Dart and Sea Wolf could strengthen carrier air defence and release frigates for anti-submarine work.
segments.question: What do you think of the stretched Type 22s?
segments.answerShort: The broad-beamed Type 22s were a good design.

segments.title: James Cable beyond Corbett and Mahan
segments.body: Britain's Naval Future and Gunboat Diplomacy are especially recommended for readers seeking naval theory beyond Corbett and Mahan. Cable is the personal favourite among the theorists discussed. His books were often cheaper at the time of this 2021 recommendation because he was less widely known.

evidence.note: A personal recommendation of James Cable, Britain's Naval Future and Gunboat Diplomacy alongside the better-known Corbett and Mahan.

segments.summary: Britain's Naval Future and Gunboat Diplomacy provide recommended reading beyond the familiar Corbett and Mahan pairing.

segments.title: What role did Argentine Canberras play in the Falklands War?
segments.body: Reconnaissance was the Argentine Canberras' most useful contribution in this assessment of their Falklands War role. They are judged to have done little beyond that, so their presence is given limited weight as a threat to the British force.

evidence.note: A limited assessment of the Argentine Canberras' threat, with reconnaissance identified as their useful role.

segments.summary: The Argentine Canberras are judged useful for reconnaissance and credited with little contribution beyond that role.
segments.question: How much of a threat were Argentine Canberra aircraft during the Falklands War?
segments.answerShort: Their reconnaissance work was useful, but they are judged to have contributed little beyond it.

segments.title: How the Landing Craft Assault balanced beaching, protection, and troop movement
segments.body: The Landing Craft Assault's hull combined a curved sheer with a more steeply curved lower bow intended to beach gently on shores of different slopes. Its angular chine construction came from powerboat practice, while the flat bow accommodated a landing ramp. Slight angles in the bottom softened pitching impacts, and longitudinal wooden battens beneath the hull helped it lie level when grounded. Outward-sloping sides helped produce a righting motion when the boat heeled. The four-and-a-half-foot ramp allowed two files of troops to leave together and used pulleys and small rollers to assist operation and withdrawal from the beach. Armoured doors separated the raised ramp area from the troop compartment. Troops sat on three longitudinal benches, with the central row exposed unless an awning was fitted and the outer rows partly sheltered beneath the decks.

evidence.note: Brian Lavery's account of the LCA's hull form, grounding battens, ramp, armoured doors and troop seating.

segments.summary: Brian Lavery's Landing Assault Craft relates the LCA's hull shape, grounding battens, bow ramp and seating to beaching and landing troops.

segments.title: LCA steering, armour and machinery arrangements
segments.body: The LCA's starboard steering shelter gave the coxswain a view without obstructing troop accommodation. He could stand through the roof doors for visibility or sit behind armour under heavy fire. A car-type wheel controlled steering, while telegraphs and a voice pipe carried orders to the stoker because the coxswain did not control engine speed directly. Selected navigation craft used non-magnetic armour to avoid compass deviation, and later models added radios. Opposite the steering shelter, a Lewis or Bren gun position combined frontal protection with sloped side panels that allowed anti-aircraft fire. Its front armour, the steering compartment and the bow doors formed a continuous barrier. A removable central bench allowed stores carriage, and a watertight bulkhead separated the troop space from the engine room.

evidence.note: Coxswain visibility and protection, indirect engine control, compass-safe armour, radio and gun positions, removable seating and engine-room separation.

segments.summary: The LCA gave its coxswain adjustable protection and indirect engine control, while armour, communications and removable seating supported assault and cargo duties.

segments.title: Could D-Day be classified as a giant river crossing?
segments.body: Large-lake operations complicate the usual distinction between amphibious assaults mounted from the sea and crossings launched from land. D-Day began on land and crossed water to another shore. On that narrowly technical basis, it can be compared with a very large river crossing. Normandy remains conventionally classified and studied as an amphibious operation.

evidence.note: Northern Italian lake crossings prompt the qualified D-Day analogy and explicit recognition of Normandy's conventional amphibious classification.

segments.summary: D-Day's launch from land permits a technical river-crossing analogy, while Normandy remains conventionally classified as an amphibious operation.
segments.question: Do large lake and river crossings count as amphibious operations, and could D-Day technically be treated as a river crossing?
segments.answerShort: Convention calls D-Day amphibious, but because it launched from land and crossed water to another shore, it can technically be compared with a very large river crossing.

segments.title: Were troops protected inside a Landing Craft Assault?
segments.body: Troops did not occupy a fully covered compartment. Men seated along the sides could shelter beneath the adjacent deck overhang. The protection therefore depended on where they sat.

evidence.note: Side-bench positions allowed some shelter beneath the adjacent hull and deck structure.

segments.summary: Men on the outer benches could tuck beneath the side decks, although the troop compartment was not fully covered.
segments.question: Were soldiers inside the Landing Craft Assault partially covered?
segments.answerShort: The compartment was not fully covered, but troops on the outer benches could shelter beneath the side decks.

segments.title: Northrop's 3A, Vought's Model 143, and the Zero ancestry myth
segments.body: When Curtiss refused to allow more development time, Jack Northrop gathered the 3A fighter's drawings and sold the package to Chance Vought. Vought used the material in its Model 143 and gained experience from Northrop's stressed-skin work, even though the aircraft lost the ensuing competition. Modified Model 143 plans and tooling were later sold to Japan. In his memoir, Heinemann rejects the later belief that the Zero descended from that transfer because its development was already well advanced.

evidence.note: Heinemann describes the Northrop 3A package passing to Chance Vought, the later sale of modified Model 143 material to Japan, and his rejection of a claimed design lineage to the Zero.

segments.summary: Heinemann recalls how Northrop's 3A design package passed to Chance Vought and later to Japan, while rejecting the claim that it became the Mitsubishi A6M Zero.

segments.title: The XBT-1 specification for vertical carrier dive bombing
segments.body: The Navy required a carrier dive bomber that could descend vertically with zero lift while speed brakes held it below 250 knots. It had to withstand a nine-g pullout with a thousand-pound bomb and carry a mechanism that displaced the weapon clear of the propeller arc. The attack began at about 20,000 feet, with the pilot extending the brakes and progressively steepening the dive while tracking the target. Bomb release at 3,000 feet was followed immediately by a pullout that imposed heavy loads on the airframe. Target movement and wind added to the pilot's task. For Heinemann, designing brakes large enough to control the descent was a central uncertainty at the outset.

evidence.note: Navy dive-bomber requirements, 250-knot dive limit, nine-g pullout, bomb clearance, attack altitudes and Heinemann's concern about brake size.

segments.summary: A thousand-pound bomb, nine-g pullout and 250-knot vertical dive made brake design and structural strength central to the Navy's new carrier bomber.

segments.title: Pricing the XBT-1 through engineering experience
segments.body: Heinemann and Northrop took their weight estimates and proposal to experienced Douglas staff to price a single aircraft. After a brief review, the cost emerged as $64,000. Heinemann was surprised by the speed of the decision, while Northrop attributed it to roughly fifteen years of experience. Fifteen years later, Heinemann was estimating contracts many times that size and understood how experienced engineers could judge a proposal so quickly.

evidence.note: Heinemann's recollection of the $64,000 estimate and his later understanding of experienced contract costing.

segments.summary: Heinemann's surprise at a rapid $64,000 estimate becomes a recollection about the practical judgment acquired through years of aircraft development.

segments.title: Making the XBT-1's flaps serve as landing aids and dive brakes
segments.body: The XBT-1 used a layout related to the A-17, with a 42-foot wingspan, partially retractable landing gear and a rear observer-gunner position. Its split trailing-edge flaps had to perform different jobs during landing and diving. A double concentric-cylinder hydraulic mechanism allowed the lower flap to extend alone for takeoff and landing, or both upper and lower surfaces to open for a dive. Careful synchronization prevented flap deployment from disturbing longitudinal trim. Heinemann adapted the principles of a Scott Russell linkage, and the arrangement gave relatively little trouble during the first year of development.

evidence.note: XBT-1 layout, alternate split-flap operating modes, hydraulic control and Scott Russell linkage principles for trim control.

segments.summary: Separate landing and dive-brake modes required synchronized flap movement so deployment would not upset the XBT-1's trim.

segments.title: Photographing the XBT-1's dangerous tail flutter
segments.body: The XBT-1 handled well in level flight, but progressively steeper dives with the brakes open produced severe tail flutter. Heinemann rode behind the test pilot and photographed the tail during repeated dives and nine-g pullouts. His measurements indicated that the horizontal tail tips moved through about two feet. Airflow vortices behind the open flaps disrupted the aircraft's stability, while the tail's strength kept the vibration from tearing it away. Rounding parts of the flap edges made little difference. The bomber could not perform its intended role unless the brakes could open without threatening structural failure or loss of control. Heinemann also recalls that designers commonly accompanied test flights before wartime practice treated the risk as unnecessary.

evidence.note: Heinemann's onboard photography, approximately two-foot tail-tip excursions, vortex diagnosis, unsuccessful edge modifications and the risks of designer participation in flight tests.

segments.summary: Repeated dives and onboard photographs revealed two-foot tail-tip movement, leaving the XBT-1 unable to use its brakes safely.

segments.title: NACA's perforated-flap solution restores a stable vertical dive
segments.body: A National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics specialist proposed cutting holes in the XBT-1's flaps to divide large vortices into smaller ones. The team had considered the idea but rejected it as too radical. Heinemann also feared that the holes would increase stalling speed beyond the 60-knot requirement dictated by carrier landings. Mechanics first cut three-inch holes in the inner third of the flaps and added more after successful tests. Once the perforations extended along the full flap, the flutter disappeared and the aircraft could descend vertically in stable flight at 250 knots. Acceptance still required persuading the Navy's bureau that the unusual perforated surfaces were satisfactory, which the project officer handled.

evidence.note: NACA advice to break up large vortices, the 60-knot stall concern, progressive perforation tests, restored 250-knot vertical flight and Navy acceptance.

segments.summary: Three-inch holes broke up the vortices behind the dive brakes, curing flutter while raising a separate concern about carrier landing speed.

segments.title: Did tanks land with the first Allied troops at Narvik?
segments.body: The tanks at Narvik came ashore well after the troops, and only a small number arrived. The shortage of tanks was one of the operation's problems. More supporting equipment would, in this judgment, have improved the Allied effort.

evidence.note: The few tanks at Narvik arrived well after the infantry, and the lack of supporting equipment limited the operation.

segments.summary: The few tanks associated with the Narvik operation arrived well after the infantry, leaving the initial landing without meaningful armoured support.
segments.question: Was Narvik the first Allied amphibious landing of the Second World War with tanks?
segments.answerShort: The tanks followed the troops much later and arrived in very small numbers.

segments.title: Castle-class corvettes ship by ship
segments.body: The Castle-class history compiled by Norman Goodwin and edited by Steve Bush traces the service movements of individual ships. Its chronological records resemble the regular naval disposition lists known as pink slips, allowing a reader to follow where each corvette went and what it did. Dumbarton Castle provides an example, moving from working up to B5 Escort Group in April 1944. Her movements during an intervening period are unreported, with spare-escort employment offered as a probable explanation. With B5 she escorted eight convoys comprising 206 ships without a loss to enemy action. She later served with a reduced complement on air-sea rescue duties, underwent a 1946 refit and entered reserve.

evidence.note: The class history's individual movement records and Dumbarton Castle's working up, uncertain employment gap, convoy totals, rescue duties and reserve service.

segments.summary: Dumbarton Castle's record connects working up, an uncertain gap in movements, eight successful convoy escorts and postwar reserve service.

segments.title: Dumbarton Castle's officers and a disputed propeller improvement
segments.body: A junior officer joining Dumbarton Castle recalls a commanding officer, Broadhead, with merchant-service experience and a career in maritime law. Broadhead assigned navigation and anti-submarine responsibilities and sent the officers on short specialist courses. Sea trials then led to the ship's working-up period. Before departure, Broadhead proposed changing the propeller pitch to gain about one and a half knots, approximately ten per cent of the ship's speed. The initial official reply dismissed his intervention. In the memoir, the eventual pitch change proved his proposal correct.

evidence.note: A junior officer's recollection of initial assignments, specialist courses, sea trials and Broadhead's initially rejected propeller-pitch proposal.

segments.summary: A commissioning memoir pairs specialist officer training with Broadhead's proposal to improve the corvette's speed by changing propeller pitch.

segments.title: Monkey Stephenson's working-up drills demanded initiative
segments.body: The Dumbarton Castle junior officer remembers Gilbert 'Monkey' Stephenson turning ship visits into sudden emergencies. Officers could be told that the captain was dead, a fire had broken out and a mine threatened the bow, then ordered to act. Stephenson demanded that officers make their men think and sent those he judged inefficient for extended retraining. Nighttime attempts to steal ships' logs tested vigilance. When an officer reversed the exercise by boarding Stephenson's own ship and claiming to have captured it, Stephenson was delighted by the initiative.

evidence.note: The junior officer's recollection of Stephenson's emergency drills, retraining, nighttime vigilance tests and approval of a counter-raid against his own ship.

segments.summary: Emergency drills, surprise night visits and enforced retraining tested whether escort officers could respond and make their crews think.

segments.title: Gibraltar convoys, escort carriers and refuelling duties
segments.body: Dumbarton Castle joined B5 Escort Group and moved from anti-submarine patrols to Gibraltar convoy work. The junior officer recalls a route extending to 30 degrees west before turning north or south to avoid German aircraft. The corvette often accompanied an escort carrier as it turned into wind to launch or recover aircraft, and landing accidents were frequent. Other assignments included escorting tankers between convoys so they could refuel the escorts. The convoys normally moved at eight knots, with weather and stragglers reducing that speed. A Gibraltar round trip usually took about five weeks, followed by a week alongside while boiler cleaning proceeded.

evidence.note: B5 assignment, the western convoy route, escort-carrier flying, tanker protection and convoy speed.
Five-week Gibraltar round trips followed by a week alongside for boiler cleaning.

segments.summary: Gibraltar escort work combined a wide Atlantic route, carrier flying support, tanker movements and recurring boiler maintenance.

segments.title: Operating ASDIC and Squid aboard Dumbarton Castle
segments.body: The anti-submarine officer's action station lay in the ASDIC compartment abaft the bridge. A leading hand and three able seamen operated the bearing, range and depth recorders. Dumbarton Castle was among the early ships fitted with the ahead-firing Squid weapon. Her main ASDIC dome could not retract into the hull and had to be raised or lowered using a small derrick on the upper deck. The junior officer recalls taking so long over the first lowering operation that the ship missed the tide on her maiden voyage.

evidence.note: ASDIC team and recorders, early Squid fitting, external dome handling and the officer's recollection of missing the tide.

segments.summary: Squid and ASDIC depended on a small specialist team, while awkward external sonar-dome handling could delay the ship's departure.

segments.title: A smallpox warning prompts vaccination at sea
segments.body: A signal warned Dumbarton Castle of a smallpox outbreak in Gibraltar and barred shore access without recent vaccination. A Polish Air Force doctor travelling as a passenger was able to vaccinate the ship's company. The junior officer's memoir recalls the use of sewing needles sterilized in a candle flame.

evidence.note: The junior officer's recollection of Gibraltar's smallpox warning and improvised vaccination by a Polish doctor travelling aboard.

segments.summary: A passenger doctor vaccinated Dumbarton Castle's crew after a smallpox warning made recent vaccination a condition for going ashore in Gibraltar.

segments.title: Edward I's castles around north Wales
segments.body: Edward I built numerous castles around north Wales, including Conwy. The group is tentatively identified as a ring of stone or stone curtain, with the label said to vary between historians.

evidence.note: Conwy Castle, Edward I's north Wales fortifications and tentatively recalled labels for the group.

segments.summary: Conwy was part of Edward I's extensive castle building around north Wales.

segments.title: Why do Castle-class corvette totals look inconsistent?
segments.body: The class history contains 39 entries with HMS, HMCS and HNoMS prefixes, rather than the fourteen ships suggested in the question. The entries span Royal Navy, Royal Canadian Navy and Royal Norwegian Navy service. The viewer then notices additional tables on the reference page they had consulted. The discrepancy comes from treating one table as the complete list.

evidence.note: A count of 39 class-history entries across three navies and the viewer's discovery of previously overlooked tables.

segments.summary: A fourteen-ship figure is corrected by checking a class history that lists 39 entries across British, Canadian, and Norwegian naval service.
segments.question: Were only fourteen Castle-class corvettes completed?
segments.answerShort: The class history lists 39 entries across British, Canadian, and Norwegian service; the apparent fourteen-ship total came from overlooking additional tables.

segments.title: When did electric searchlights appear on warships?
segments.body: The Royal Navy used searchlights at Alexandria in 1882 to prevent Egyptian forces from manning artillery batteries. U.S. Navy attempts to fit them appear to date to about the preceding year. British fittings may have been contemporary with those American experiments, so the order of adoption remains uncertain. Searchlights were reportedly also used during the siege of Paris.

evidence.note: Royal Navy operational use at Alexandria in 1882, tentative American fitting dates, uncertainty over priority and reported use during the siege of Paris.

segments.summary: Alexandria supplies a clear Royal Navy operational example from 1882, while American fitting experiments appear slightly earlier and the first adopter remains uncertain.
segments.question: When did electric searchlights begin appearing on warships?
segments.answerShort: Royal Navy operational use is documented at Alexandria in 1882, while the U.S. Navy appears to have experimented with fittings around 1881.

segments.title: Japan's C1 attack submarines and their midget-submarine fittings
segments.body: The C-class attack boats were intended to work with A-type command submarines and B-type scouts. Their design developed the KD6 layout with two additional torpedo tubes, giving eight forward tubes in two torpedo rooms arranged one above the other. The C1 boats carried twenty torpedoes, a 5.5-inch deck gun and a twin 25 mm anti-aircraft mounting. They carried no aircraft, but fittings aft of the conning tower accommodated a Type A midget submarine. The design also offered improved underwater manoeuvrability over the KD6. In early 1943, I-16's conversion to supply work removed the deck gun and reduced torpedo reloads.

evidence.note: The C1 design's relationship to A/B-type roles and KD6, eight-tube armament, midget-submarine fittings and I-16 supply conversion.

segments.summary: Eight bow torpedo tubes and midget-submarine fittings gave Japan's C1 boats a concentrated attack role, before supply conversions reduced their armament.

segments.title: C1 operations from Pearl Harbor to supply missions and losses
segments.body: All five C1 boats carried midget submarines for the Pearl Harbor attack. Three later deployed to the Indian Ocean, where their midgets damaged a British battleship and sank a tanker, while the parent submarines subsequently sank fourteen freighters as commerce raiders. Further midget attacks off Guadalcanal damaged only one U.S. Navy transport. I-22 and I-24 carried midgets for the Sydney attack, whose limited result was the sinking of an old accommodation ferry. The boats also undertook supply missions as the war continued. I-18, I-16 and I-20 were lost to U.S. destroyers, and I-22 went missing in the eastern Solomons. I-24, a submarine of about 2,500 tons, was rammed and sunk off the Aleutians by a 675-ton submarine chaser.

evidence.note: C1 midget deployments, Indian Ocean commerce raiding, limited Guadalcanal and Sydney results, supply employment and the five boats' losses or disappearance.

segments.summary: The C1 boats combined distant midget attacks and commerce raiding with supply missions before all five were lost or went missing.

segments.title: Supermarine's unexpected naval aircraft proposals beyond the Spitfire
segments.body: Supermarine's proposed aircraft extended well beyond the designs that entered service. One proposal was a twin-engined biplane with a monocoque fuselage, offered as an answer to the requirement associated with the Fairey Swordfish. It fits a recurring interest in persuading the Royal Navy to adopt a twin-engined aircraft. The carrier drawn beneath it appears fanciful: a fixed raised gun position on the flight deck would obstruct the clear working surface required for aircraft. A possible naval fighter is absent from the book, leaving that project unresolved.

evidence.note: Supermarine's unbuilt proposals, a twin-engined biplane, criticism of a carrier illustration's flight-deck obstruction and the absence of a proposed naval fighter.

segments.summary: Beyond the Spitfire reveals Supermarine studies for naval service, including a twin-engined biplane intended to answer the same requirement that produced the Swordfish.

segments.title: Frank Whittle's RAF service and Power Jets
segments.body: Dr Clarke initially treats Frank Whittle as an RAF officer assigned temporarily to companies, while admitting that he would need to check those attachments. Whittle's RAF service to 1948 and rank of air commodore are offered in support of that interpretation. A viewer then brings up Power Jets, formed with two colleagues to develop his engine ideas, and its nationalization in 1944. The company attachments therefore remain uncertain in this account.

evidence.note: Initial account of Whittle's RAF affiliation and work with several companies.
Uncertain company attachments, an explicit need to check, RAF service to 1948, and air commodore rank.
A viewer's Power Jets correction and the stated 1944 nationalization, with uncertainty over the founding year.

segments.summary: Whittle's company attachments remain uncertain as his RAF service is compared with the history of Power Jets.

segments.title: Mitchell's biplane benchmark and the road to the F.7/30 fighter
segments.body: Mitchell intended to submit a monoplane but developed a conventional biplane alongside it as a backup and reference design. Both used the Rolls-Royce Goshawk, then called the Kestrel S, with evaporative cooling intended to reduce weight and drag. Joint work on Schneider Trophy racers had given Mitchell confidence in Rolls-Royce's experimental department. Surviving layout drawings dated February 1931 followed preliminary wind-tunnel work and preceded the formal F.7/30 specification, while the Air Ministry had already signalled its engine preference. The biplane incorporated wing condensers, four proposed Vickers guns, bomb racks, and measures to improve the pilot's view. Its thin lower wings raised doubts about fitting their guns without substantial blisters or fairings. Because the monoplane remained the principal design, the biplane may have served mainly as a benchmark.

evidence.note: Parallel fighter studies, Goshawk evaporative cooling, Schneider Trophy experience, early drawings and wind-tunnel work, and Air Ministry signals before the formal specification.
Biplane structure, pilot visibility, condenser placement, proposed guns and bomb racks, gun-installation doubts, and its possible benchmark role.

segments.summary: R. J. Mitchell developed biplane and monoplane studies in parallel, using Rolls-Royce evaporative cooling and early wind-tunnel work before the F.7/30 requirement formally appeared.

segments.title: How good might a Supermarine Swordfish have been?
segments.body: Reliability and the ability to produce sufficient numbers are offered as probable reasons for choosing Fairey's Swordfish. A Supermarine alternative receives a favourable initial reaction, but its possible performance remains unexplored. Blackburn's later production of the Fairey aircraft receives a brief mention.

evidence.note: A Supermarine Swordfish counterfactual, probable reliability and production considerations behind the Fairey choice, and a brief Blackburn production reference.

segments.summary: Reliability and production capacity are suggested reasons for the Royal Navy's choice of Fairey's Swordfish.
segments.question: How good might a Supermarine alternative to the Fairey Swordfish have been?
segments.answerShort: It sounds appealing, but reliability and the ability to produce enough aircraft are suggested reasons for the Fairey choice.

segments.title: Why aircraft project lists can remain incomplete
segments.body: A published history can leave part of an aircraft designer's work unaccounted for. Classified government projects are one possible source of gaps. Studies that never progressed beyond the drawing board can also disappear from a list if the compiler does not regard them as proper projects. For unusually productive designers and teams, a complete-looking inventory therefore warrants caution. The total can remain approximate without particular missing aircraft having been identified.

evidence.note: Skepticism about complete aircraft-project inventories because classified work and drawing-board studies can be omitted.

segments.summary: Classified work and abandoned drawing-board studies can leave gaps even in apparently complete aircraft-design inventories.

segments.title: U.S. Marine Corps aviation and the Corsair's reputation
segments.body: U.S. Marine Corps Aviation Since 1912 provides a reference history of the service's aircraft. The Corsair's strong association with the Marines prompts a comparison with the Royal Navy's role in developing it into the fighter remembered from later service. That comparison credits British interest while characterizing the Marines' initial reception as less enthusiastic. The fourth edition includes a foreword by John H. Glenn.

evidence.note: The Marine aviation history, its 1912 starting point and fourth edition, the Corsair comparison, and John H. Glenn's foreword.

segments.summary: A history beginning in 1912 introduces Marine aviation through the Corsair and the Royal Navy's contribution to its development.

segments.title: The Panther, swept-wing Cougar, and Marine aviation roles
segments.body: The F9F Panther continued in service after establishing a reputation for toughness in Korea. The F9F-6 changed enough to receive the Cougar name, with a prototype using 35-degree swept wings. Production moved beyond the straight-wing Panther into successive Cougar versions, including a two-seat aircraft and a long-nosed photographic variant. The two-seater was the only Cougar version described as seeing combat, serving Marine forward air control in Vietnam. Other Marine Cougar assignments included attack and photographic reconnaissance work. Manufacturer naming families such as Grumman's cats, Douglas's Sky prefix, and McDonnell's supernatural names helped create recognizable identities.

evidence.note: Panther service after Korea, Cougar swept-wing development, two-seat and photographic variants, Marine roles, and aircraft naming families.

segments.summary: Swept wings turned the Panther lineage into the Cougar, whose Marine roles included reconnaissance, attack, and forward air control.

segments.title: Marine squadrons and the early transition to carrier jets
segments.body: A Marine squadron returning from Korea changed aircraft during the following year. Its Corsairs gave way to Panthers before the North American FJ2 Fury arrived. The FJ2 is described as essentially a navalized F-86. The earlier straight-wing FJ1 had served only briefly and in small numbers. Alongside the FH1 Phantom, its principal purpose was to introduce the Navy to jet operations from carriers. Following this transition requires attention to changing unit designations as well as aircraft names.

evidence.note: A Marine squadron's Corsair/Panther/FJ2 progression, designation changes, and the earlier FJ1 and FH1 role in introducing carrier-jet operations.

segments.summary: A Marine squadron's move from Corsairs through Panthers to FJ2 Furys sits within the Navy's wider introduction to carrier jets.

segments.title: British submarine production, the A class, and special-purpose designs
segments.body: The S, U, and T classes provided the basis for British submarines completed in time for wartime operations. Improvements from combat experience entered those designs as building capacity allowed. Several proposed special-purpose designs were deferred because their advantages did not justify disruption to the construction programme. Work on the A class went ahead from late 1941, with introduction planned for a point when builders could accommodate it. A-class boats were about to be delivered at frequent intervals when the war ended, and they formed the basis of the postwar fleet. Introducing that generation is offered as evidence of continued British naval ambition despite financial strain. X and XE midget submarines and Chariot human torpedoes demanded design effort disproportionate to their size, although the 1947 paper judges that investment worthwhile.

evidence.note: The 1947 paper's account of submarine design continuity, construction constraints, the A-class programme, and design effort for X/XE craft and Chariots, followed by an interpretation of Britain's continuing naval ambitions.

segments.summary: Wartime submarine development balanced improvements against disruption to construction, with the A class and small special-purpose craft making different demands on designers.

segments.title: S-class submarines: welding, armament, and Far Eastern endurance
segments.body: S-class submarines were designed for offensive patrols in confined waters such as the North Sea and Mediterranean. Small prewar orders allowed repeated improvements, and early wartime experience supported further construction because the class suited North Sea operations and was economical to build. Progress from riveting to welding improved hull robustness and permitted greater diving depth. An added stern-firing external torpedo tube was omitted from some boats when a 4-inch gun replaced their 3-inch weapon. Far Eastern operations required more endurance, leading to the conversion of some main ballast tanks into fuel tanks. Riveted external tanks had leaked when structures worked or ships bumped alongside, risking an oil trail that could reveal a submarine. Welded tanks largely removed that obstacle to carrying fuel outside the pressure hull.

evidence.note: S-class patrol requirements, iterative construction, welding and diving depth, stern-tube/gun choices, and external fuel tanks for Far Eastern range.

segments.summary: Welding improved S-class hulls and made external fuel stowage practical, helping adapt a confined-water patrol submarine for longer voyages.

segments.title: U-class submarines: simple machinery and revised bow arrangements
segments.body: The original U class was intended to replace H-class training boats while also providing short-distance wartime patrols. Its simple diesel-electric machinery helped rapid production, and limited operational capability still proved well suited to Mediterranean work from Malta. External bow torpedo tubes gave the early boats a bluff forward shape that complicated periscope-depth keeping, produced a prominent bow wave, and reduced speed in a seaway. Later boats received a finer bow, while additional operational equipment made it necessary to forgo those external tubes. A quick-diving tank improved diving and control during torpedo firing by allowing the boat to be made deliberately heavy. Later construction used more welding, but the pressure-hull plating seams remained riveted throughout the class.

evidence.note: U-class training and patrol origins, production advantages, Malta operations, bow-tube drawbacks, quick-diving tanks, and the limit of wartime welding adoption.

segments.summary: U-class production benefited from simple machinery, while revised bows and quick-diving tanks addressed handling and firing problems.

segments.title: T-class submarines: construction priorities and a stern-firing salvo
segments.body: The T class replaced older patrol submarines, with Triton in the 1935 programme and only three boats completed when war began. More boats were wanted, but the need for numbers diverted some construction toward the easier U and S classes. T-class orders ceased once preparations for the A class were sufficiently advanced. Complete welding improved hull strength, and conversion of main tanks to fuel stowage increased endurance for Far Eastern work. Revised bow casings reduced the blunt shape around the forward external torpedo tubes. Amidships external tubes changed from firing forward to firing aft, and a later additional tube at the rear of the casing strengthened the stern-firing salvo.

evidence.note: T-class replacement role, construction competition with smaller classes, the A-class transition, welded hulls, extra fuel, and changed external torpedo-tube directions.

segments.summary: The T class combined patrol capability with revised torpedo arcs, while wartime demand for numbers limited construction of the larger boats.

segments.title: Black Swan-class sloops through builders' plans
segments.body: Builders' plans can be compared by frame positions to reconstruct the ships' arrangement in three dimensions. Amethyst and Starling carried the same three twin 4-inch mountings, but their ready-use lockers and several smaller weapons arrangements differed. Their quarterdeck depth-charge rails and throwers followed the same layout, while spare-charge stowage varied and Amethyst carried a split Hedgehog anti-submarine mortar. The comparison also identifies different Oerlikon mounts, radar supports, searchlights, and positions for smoke floats. Even where accommodation and lower-deck arrangements were similar, Amethyst used part of a ballast-tank space for small-arms ammunition. These details distinguish individual ships within the class instead of treating one set of plans as representative of every sloop.

evidence.note: Matching plan frames for reconstruction and the stated Amethyst/Starling differences in light weapons, Hedgehog, ready-use lockers, radar supports, searchlights, smoke floats, and ammunition stowage.
