segments.summary: Detailed builders' plans expose the Black Swan class's internal arrangement, weapons, depth-charge gear, Hedgehog mortar, and ship-to-ship differences.

segments.title: A contemporary guide to the late Soviet Navy
segments.body: Norman Polmar's fifth edition of Guide to the Soviet Navy was published in 1991, while the Soviet Navy still existed. It provides a contemporary view of a fleet valued here for its lessons in naval history. Its amphibious-warfare section supplies the next ship examples.

evidence.note: Norman Polmar's fifth edition, its stated 1991 publication date, and the transition into amphibious warfare ships.

segments.summary: Norman Polmar's fifth edition records the Soviet Navy near the end of the Cold War and introduces a reading on amphibious ships.

segments.title: Ivan Rogov combines beaching, docking, helicopters, and heavy weapons
segments.body: The Ivan Rogov class could carry a naval infantry battalion with its vehicles and equipment. Bow doors and a flat-bottomed tank deck supported unloading amphibious vehicles into the water or across a beach, while a floodable docking well carried conventional or air-cushion landing craft. A hangar accommodated four helicopters, which could pass through the superstructure and down a ramp to the forward landing area because the funnel uptakes were split around their route. Air-defence missiles, dual-purpose guns, close-in weapons, and a 122 mm barrage-rocket launcher provided armament and landing support. The three ships were completed in 1978, 1982, and 1989, with four years between the first two and seven between the second and third. The guide also follows their assignments to the Pacific and Baltic fleets and the lead ship's return for the 1981 Zapad amphibious exercises.

evidence.note: The Ivan Rogov entry's troop capacity, helicopter passage, bow and well-deck arrangements, armament, completion dates, fleet assignments, and 1981 amphibious exercises.

segments.summary: The Ivan Rogov-class entry shows a Soviet landing ship designed to beach vehicles, operate landing craft from a well deck, fly helicopters, and defend itself with missiles, guns, and rockets.

segments.title: Soviet amphibious capacity and the limits of listed troop numbers
segments.body: The 1991 guide describes a slight decline in the number of Soviet amphibious ships while additional landing ships were still under construction in Poland. Political and economic changes there made further construction uncertain. Large air-cushion landing craft and wing-in-ground-effect vehicles were increasing short-range amphibious capacity. Apart from the Ivan Rogov class, the large landing ships described had been built in Poland. Published troop capacities counted the personnel for whom berths were provided, so ships could carry more troops on short crossings when everyone did not require a sleeping place.

evidence.note: The guide's contemporary construction outlook, Polish shipbuilding, short-range air-cushion and ground-effect craft, and berth-based troop capacity figures.

segments.summary: A 1991 fleet assessment separates ship numbers from short-range lift and explains why berth counts can understate troops carried on brief crossings.

segments.title: How might Western Cold War fleets better counter the Soviet Navy?
segments.body: The counterfactual begins with an earlier introduction of close-in weapon systems. Its larger shipbuilding choices depend on knowing whether the Cold War will remain a global contest for presence or become a shooting war. Under the first assumption, modified Type 82 destroyers combining Sea Dart and Sea Wolf would provide the Royal Navy with larger ships for worldwide commitments. The American alternative would retain a larger cruiser above the mass-produced destroyer, rather than treating the Ticonderoga as sufficient for that role. Diesel-electric submarines would complement nuclear boats by concentrating on northern barriers while the latter handled long-range operations. Quiet electric running would complicate Soviet anti-submarine operations and help threaten movements down the Norwegian coast. Continuing the existing Type 42 production programme was easier than making a fresh design choice.

evidence.note: Earlier close-in weapons, the global-presence assumption, modified Type 82 and larger American cruiser alternatives, diesel-submarine barriers, and continued Type 42 production.

segments.summary: A Cold War counterfactual combines larger ships for global presence with quiet diesel submarines for northern barriers.
segments.question: Knowing what is known now, what changes would improve Royal Navy and U.S. Navy fleets against the Soviet Navy?
segments.answerShort: Introduce close-in defenses earlier, build larger British and American surface combatants, and retain quiet diesel submarines for chokepoint and barrier operations.

segments.title: Stalin's purges and Red Army readiness in 1941
segments.body: Stalin's purges removed many experienced Red Army officers before the army faced Germany in the Second World War. Replacing experience with political reliability weakened its senior leadership at the start of the fighting. An opponent gains when a state destroys its own officer corps. Political paranoia therefore damaged battlefield readiness and contributed to the Red Army's early wartime difficulties.

evidence.note: Loss of experienced officers through Stalin's purges and its connection to early Red Army difficulties against Germany.

segments.summary: Stalin's purges weakened the Red Army's experienced leadership before its fighting against Germany.

segments.title: Kirov-class ships, submarine threats, and a naval arms-race counterfactual
segments.body: Additional British Type 82s provide the premise for a counterfactual in which larger Western ships encourage expensive Soviet attempts to exceed them. Kirovs are treated as costly concentrations of resources that Royal Navy submarines would make priority targets. Spearfish torpedoes are mentioned, with the older Mark 8 and the Conqueror-Belgrano example illustrating the same submarine threat. This assessment expresses less concern about the ships than some competing views and stresses their economic burden on the Soviet fleet.

evidence.note: The Type 82/Kirov follow-up question, a counterfactual competitive-building response, Royal Navy submarine priority targeting, and the stated Soviet resource burden.

segments.summary: A Type 82 counterfactual leads to an assessment of Kirovs as expensive Soviet assets exposed to concentrated submarine attention.
segments.question: With more Type 82s coming into service, would the Kirovs have been taken more seriously?
segments.answerShort: Their cost and priority as submarine targets receive greater emphasis, alongside the possibility that larger Western ships could stimulate further Soviet spending.

segments.title: A stronger prewar British anti-submarine fleet
segments.body: The proposed programme would build inexpensive, treaty-exempt sloops steadily from 1928 and keep usable ships in reserve. One sloop would accompany each destroyer ordered, producing an annual escort flotilla alongside the destroyer flotilla. Those ships would support minesweeping and anti-submarine work while remaining within the stated speed and armament restrictions. The intention is to have a substantial escort force available before wartime demand exposes the shortage. Suitable merchant ships would also be built with rapid conversion into escort carriers in mind.

evidence.note: A hypothetical one-for-one sloop and destroyer programme from 1928, reserve hulls, minesweeping and anti-submarine roles, treaty limits, and merchant escort-carrier preparation.

segments.summary: The proposed interwar program pairs every destroyer flotilla with mass-produced sloops and prepares suitable merchant hulls for rapid escort-carrier conversion.
segments.question: What changes would have improved Britain's anti-submarine fleet before and during the Second World War?
segments.answerShort: Begin mass-producing versatile sloops much earlier, match them to destroyer construction, and prepare merchant hulls for rapid escort-carrier conversion.

segments.title: Littoral Strike Ships and expanding requirements
segments.body: The Royal Navy concept under consideration in 2021 is a Littoral Strike Ship, abbreviated LSS. Its initial role is a special-operations platform able to carry roughly a company of Marines. Proposals for more troops raise further questions about helicopter or fixed-wing support and the weight of vehicles to be carried. The concept described lacks the ability to land vehicles, a limitation judged particularly awkward for smaller forces needing vehicles of their own. Its eventual form therefore remains uncertain.

evidence.note: The LCS/LSS distinction, initial special-operations role, proposed troop increases, aviation choices, and unresolved vehicle-landing requirements.

segments.summary: The 2021 Littoral Strike Ship concept faces unresolved demands for more Marines, vehicles, landing craft, and aviation.
segments.question: Is the Royal Navy building LCS-type ships?
segments.answerShort: The concept discussed is the Littoral Strike Ship, or LSS, initially intended for special operations and about a company of Marines.

segments.title: A common Littoral Strike Ship hull and the possibility of an LHD
segments.body: A common hull for different troop capacities receives a sceptical response without a technical comparison of the options. In the 2021 discussion, even the number of ships remains open, with three being considered instead of two. One speculative outcome is an LHD with a ski ramp, which would increase the number of British flight decks able to operate F-35s. This remains a prediction about how requirements might develop.

evidence.note: A viewer's common-hull proposal, uncertainty between two and three ships, and a speculative ski-ramp LHD outcome with additional F-35-capable decks.

segments.summary: A common-hull proposal leads to speculation about three LHD-like ships with ski ramps and additional F-35-capable decks.
segments.question: Why not use one Littoral Strike Ship hull type for different troop capacities?
segments.answerShort: The proposal receives a sceptical response without a technical comparison. Ship numbers remain uncertain, and an LHD is suggested as one possible outcome.

segments.title: Which forces were expected to use Littoral Strike Ships?
segments.body: Royal Marines and the Special Boat Service are identified as the expected users of the proposed Littoral Strike Ships. Special Air Service participation is treated as possible. The suggestion that the Parachute Regiment would use them receives a doubtful response.

evidence.note: Royal Marines and SBS are identified, SAS participation remains possible, and Parachute Regiment involvement is doubted.

segments.summary: The expected users are Royal Marines and SBS, with possible SAS involvement and doubt about the Parachute Regiment.
segments.question: Were Littoral Strike Ships intended for the Marines, SAS, SBS, and Parachute Regiment?
segments.answerShort: Royal Marines and SBS are identified, SAS is possible, and Parachute Regiment involvement is doubted.
